title: Texas 2026 Midterm Results: Key Local Races Unveiled – CBS News Exclusive
body:
The night after Texas voters headed to the polls, former President Donald J. Trump took a surprising turn on a live CBS interview, offering congratulations to the Democratic candidates who were poised to win key statewide contests and pledging to work with the new lawmakers. The remarks came as the first precincts in North Texas began reporting results for a slate of tightly contested races that could reshape the political balance in the Lone Star State and have reverberations across the national midterm landscape.

In the early hours of Tuesday, polls in most of North Texas were slated to close at 7 p.m. Central Time, setting the stage for a rapid cascade of vote tallies that would determine the fate of several high‑profile contests. Among them were the race for the open U.S. Senate seat left vacant by the retirement of Republican incumbent John Cornyn, a fiercely fought battle for the state’s 2nd Congressional District, and a pivotal contest for the Texas Railroad Commission, a body that regulates the state’s booming oil and gas industry. As the first precincts reported, Democrats made unexpected inroads, narrowing margins that had long been considered safe for Republicans.

Trump’s congratulatory tone was unexpected given his historically combative post‑election rhetoric. In the interview, the former president said, “I want to congratulate the Democrats who have won in Texas. We have a great country and we will work together.” He added that his administration would continue to support policies that benefit Texas, such as energy development and border security, regardless of which party held office. Political analysts noted that the remarks could be an attempt to soften the partisan divide ahead of a Congress that is expected to be sharply split, and to position Trump as a pragmatic figure capable of bipartisan cooperation.

The emerging results underscore a broader shift in Texas politics that has been brewing for years. Demographic changes, including rapid growth in suburban areas around Dallas‑Fort Worth and an influx of younger, more diverse voters, have eroded the Republican stronghold that once seemed unassailable. In the 2nd Congressional District, for instance, a Democrat who had previously trailed by double digits in mid‑term polls now finds the race within single‑digit range, buoyed by strong turnout among Hispanic and Asian American communities. Similarly, the Senate contest, once projected as a clear Republican victory, is now a toss‑up, with exit polls indicating that independent voters are gravitating toward the Democratic challenger’s moderate platform on energy policy and education.

Republican strategists, however, caution against reading too much into the early numbers. They point out that Texas’s vast geography and staggered reporting can produce misleading trends in the first few hours. “We still have a long night ahead,” said a senior advisor to the Republican Senate campaign. “Rural counties that lean heavily Republican will report later, and historically they have turned the tide in close races.” Moreover, the Republican Party is rallying its base around issues such as border security and property tax relief, hoping to re‑energize voters who may have stayed home in previous midterms.

The political implications extend beyond state borders. A Democratic gain in the Texas Senate seat would be the first for the party in the state since 1994 and could tip the balance of power in the U.S. Senate, where control is expected to hinge on a handful of competitive races nationwide. Likewise, a shift in the Railroad Commission could influence national energy policy debates, especially as the country grapples with the transition to renewable sources while maintaining energy reliability.

As the night unfolds, the final tallies will likely confirm whether Texas is indeed undergoing a partisan realignment or if the early Democratic surge will fade as later precincts report. Regardless of the outcome, Trump’s unexpected gesture of goodwill signals a new chapter in post‑election discourse, one that may encourage more collaborative politics in a deeply divided era. The coming days will reveal whether this overture translates into tangible bipartisan action in the Texas Capitol and beyond, setting the tone for the broader midterm contests that will shape the nation’s legislative agenda for the next two years.
